claims.text: A hybrid ML and lattice-distortion-correction methodology can accurately predict melting properties of high-entropy alloys.
A correction based on atomic-radius variance and valence electron concentration can compensate for errors caused by HEA lattice distortion.
Standard CALPHAD and first-principles methods struggle with the complex energy landscapes of multicomponent HEAs.
NbTaTiV can form a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
W-Ta-V-Cr can form a single-phase BCC high-entropy alloy.
Random atomic distributions in the candidate alloys produce severe lattice distortion.
Predictions from a model trained on ordered compounds can be corrected and used in modified thermodynamic integration to estimate melting temperature, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity.
Relevant high-temperature experimental data are sparse at temperatures up to 1100°C or higher.
The candidate alloy remains a single-phase BCC structure at high temperature.
Severe lattice distortion and local chemical disparity create a rough energy landscape.
The rough energy landscape equalizes defect mobilities and alters dislocation-core structures.
Standard ordered-compound models fail to capture the effects of the rough energy landscape without a correction.
Standard CALPHAD and ordered-compound ML models assume idealized or periodic atomic environments.
Random distributions of elements with different atomic radii cause wavy dislocation lines and non-neutral dislocation cores.
Atomic-radius variance and VEC govern deviations in elastic isotropy and dislocation mobility.
The hybrid method will predict melting temperatures and heat capacities with relative errors below 5%.
Standard CALPHAD or uncorrected ML models will have errors above 10–15% for the same properties.
An ordered-compound ML model predicts NbTaTiV shear and bulk moduli with errors of 2.5% and 6%, respectively.
The lattice-distortion effect may reduce the accuracy of ordered-compound models for HEAs, but insufficient data prevent assessment of its magnitude.
The proposed method may fail when phase separation or kinetically dominant processes control behavior.
